summary.text: Lesson 1-3 of enVision Math Grade 4: comparing numbers by lining up places and marching from the left until the digits differ. Covers the > < = symbols, naming the deciding place, digit-count comparisons, and comparing numbers written in expanded form.

why.text: Comparing is the first place the ten-times staircase gets USED for something. The skill under test is naming which place decided — that is the reasoning teachers ask her to show, and it is also what rounding needs next lesson.

objectives.text: Compare two numbers with > < = by finding the leftmost differing place
Name the place that decides a comparison
Use digit count to compare numbers of different lengths

parentNote.text: Built from the HW 1-3 sheet. Two deliberate hard spots: one question gives correct-answer-wrong-reasoning and asks her to spot the broken step (comparing digits from different places), because her sheet asks for explanations and that is where points are lost; and one question runs the rule backwards — build a number where a NAMED place decides. Fresh scenarios throughout; her sheet's numbers were not reused.

nextUp.text: Quiz in one sitting. Say the deciding place out loud on every question — that habit is the lesson.

cards.def:
**Line up the places, start at the LEFT, and find the first place where the digits differ.**
• That one place decides the whole comparison.
• Everything to the right of it cannot change the answer.
cards.hint: Leftmost difference wins. Nothing after it matters.

cards.def:
**> means is greater than, < means is less than, = means equal.**
• 6,378 > 6,356 and 6,356 < 6,378 say the same fact both ways.
• The open side always faces the bigger number.

**A whole number with more digits is always greater than one with fewer.**
• Any 6-digit number beats any 5-digit number: even 100,000 > 99,999.
• This is why you count digits before comparing anything else.

**Rebuild each number from its parts before comparing.**
• 30,000 + 5,000 + 3 is 35,003.
• Never compare the parts one by one — one big part can beat several small ones.

**The deciding place is the leftmost one where the digits differ.**
• For 60,618 and 60,647: ten thousands match, thousands match, hundreds match — the TENS decide.
• Naming the deciding place is how you show your reasoning, not just your answer.

questions.hint: Same number of digits, so compare from the left.
steps: Both have six digits, so compare place by place from the left.
Hundred thousands: 4 = 4. Ten thousands: 2 versus 3.
2 < 3, so 428,617 < 431,502 — the ten thousands place decided it.

ex.main: **<.** The first differing place was the ten thousands, and nothing after it could change the answer.
ex.tip: The open mouth of the symbol always faces the larger number.

questions.q: Which place would you use to compare 87,309 and 87,344?
questions.hint: Walk left to right until the digits stop matching.
steps: Ten thousands: 8 = 8. Thousands: 7 = 7. Hundreds: 3 = 3.
Tens: 0 versus 4 — the first difference.
So the tens place decides: 87,309 < 87,344.

ex.main: **The tens place.** You only name the FIRST place where the digits differ.
ex.tip: Being able to name the deciding place is what the test questions ask for, not just the symbol.

opts: 10,001 is greater because it has more digits
9,999 is greater because it has more nines
steps: 9,999 has four digits. 10,001 has five.
A five-digit whole number is always greater than a four-digit one.
So 10,001 > 9,999, even though its digits look smaller.

ex.main: **10,001 is greater — more digits wins.** The size of the individual digits never overcomes an extra place.
ex.tip: The digit-count check takes one second and prevents the most tempting wrong answer in the lesson.

questions.q: Two towns report their populations: Kestrel 530,240 and Marlow 503,240. Which town is larger, and which place decided it?
opts: Kestrel — the ten thousands place decided
questions.hint: The digits look similar. March left to right carefully.
steps: Hundred thousands: 5 = 5.
Ten thousands: 3 versus 0 — the first difference.
3 > 0, so 530,240 > 503,240. Kestrel is larger.
Everything after the ten thousands place is identical, and irrelevant anyway.

ex.main: **Kestrel, decided at the ten thousands.** Transposed-looking numbers like these are exactly where careful place-marching earns its keep.
ex.tip: When two numbers share digits in a different order, the leftmost difference still settles it.

questions.hint: Rebuild both numbers first. Do not compare the pieces.
steps: Compare: thousands place is 2 versus 3, so 43,010 is greater.
The extra parts in the first number never made up for the missing thousand.

ex.main: **43,010 is greater.** One step up in a bigger place beats any pile of smaller parts.
ex.tip: Expanded-form comparisons are place-value questions in disguise. Always rebuild first.

questions.q: A number is compared to 68,314 and the hundreds place decides it. Which number could it be?
questions.hint: The deciding place is the FIRST difference — so everything left of the hundreds must match.
steps: For the hundreds to decide, the ten thousands and thousands must match 68,314: they must start 68,—.
58,314 differs at the ten thousands, so that place would decide. Out.
68,324 first differs at the tens; 68,315 at the ones. Both decided later than hundreds. Out.
68,714 matches 6 and 8, then differs at the hundreds: 7 versus 3. The hundreds decide.

ex.main: **68,714.** Building a number to order like this proves you understand the rule, not just follow it.
ex.tip: Reverse questions — build the example instead of checking one — are how this shows up on tests.

questions.q: A stadium sold 91,867 tickets on Saturday and 91,876 on Sunday. Which day sold more?
questions.hint: The digits are nearly identical. Find the first difference.
steps: Ten thousands, thousands and hundreds all match: 9, 1, 8.
Tens: 6 versus 7 — the first difference.
7 > 6, so 91,876 > 91,867. Sunday sold more.

ex.main: **Sunday.** Two numbers built from the same digits are the easiest place to rush and the best place not to.
ex.tip: Swapped neighbouring digits are a favourite trap. The left-to-right march does not fall for it.

questions.q: A student claims: "A whole number with 4 digits is always greater than a whole number with 3 digits." Is the claim true, and what is the strongest support?
opts: True — the smallest 4-digit number, 1,000, already beats the largest 3-digit number, 999
False — it depends on the digits
questions.hint: Test the claim at its weakest point: the smallest 4-digit versus the largest 3-digit.
steps: The smallest whole number with 4 digits is 1,000.
The largest whole number with 3 digits is 999.
Since 1,000 > 999, even the worst case wins — so every case wins.
Checking the extreme case is what makes this an argument rather than a guess.

ex.main: **True, and the boundary case proves it.** If the smallest of one group beats the largest of the other, no comparison can go the other way.
ex.tip: Testing a claim at its extreme is a real proof move. It shows up in every grade of math from here on.

questions.q: A classmate says: "76,842 > 76,839 because 8 > 3." The answer happens to be right. What is wrong with the reasoning?
opts: It compared digits from different places — the tens decide here, not a mismatched pair
You cannot compare numbers this close
questions.hint: Check WHICH digits the reasoning compared, and which places they came from.
steps: March left: 7 = 7, 6 = 6, 8 = 8. The hundreds MATCH.
The first difference is the tens: 4 versus 3, so 76,842 > 76,839. The answer is right.
But "8 > 3" compared the hundreds of one number to the tens of the other — different places.
Right answer, broken reasoning — on a test that asks you to explain, this loses the points.

ex.main: **The reasoning compared digits from different places.** A correct answer with wrong reasoning fails the moment the numbers change.
ex.tip: Always name the place you are comparing. It keeps the digits honest.

questions.q: Three friends measure reading minutes this month: Ana 12,408, Bo 12,480, Cami 12,048. Order them from most to least.
questions.hint: Same first two digits everywhere. The hundreds and tens sort it out.
steps: All three start 12,—, so compare the hundreds: Ana 4, Bo 4, Cami 0. Cami is last.
Ana versus Bo: hundreds tie at 4, so compare tens — Ana 0, Bo 8.
Bo 12,480 > Ana 12,408, so the order is Bo, Ana, Cami.

ex.main: **Bo, Ana, Cami.** Ordering three numbers is just the two-number compare, applied twice with care.
ex.tip: Sort out the easy separations first (Cami), then settle the close pair.
